en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Ratanavagga 91.
The Training Rule on Rain-Cloaks.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had authorized the rainy-season robes for the monks.
The group of six monks,
thinking, "The Blessed One has authorized the rainy-season robes," wore rainy-season robes of unlimited size.
They wandered about dragging [the robes] both from the front and from behind.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as above]... complained, grumbled, and were indignant, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks wear rain-cloaks of unlimited size?"... [as above]...
“Is it true, monks, that you wear large rain-cloaks?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before] ...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you wear rain-cloaks of unlimited size?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Furthermore, when a monk is having a rain-cloak made, it must be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: six spans in length by the Sugata’s span, and two and a half spans in width.
For one who exceeds that, there is an offense entailing expiation with cutting down.”
"Rain-cloak" means for the purpose of the four months of the rainy season.
"By one having it made" means...
Whether making it oneself or having it made, it should be made according to the prescribed measurement.
Herein, this is the measurement: six spans in length by the Sugata-span, and two and a half spans in width.
If one makes it or has it made exceeding that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of undertaking.
Having cut it off upon obtaining [the material], a *pācittiya* offense is to be confessed.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself through others, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If she brings to completion herself what has been half-finished by others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she brings to completion by others what has been half-finished by others, there is an offense of expiation.
If she makes it or causes it to be made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one obtains and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if one makes it according to the proper measure.
He makes it deficient;
or, having obtained something made by another that exceeds the proper measure, he cuts it down and uses it;
or he makes a canopy, a floor-covering, a screen-wall, a mattress, or a pillow.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The ninth training rule concerning the rainy-season robe is finished.
